newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-THOUSANDS STRANDED AFTER "NATIONAL" BOMB ALERT.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-THOUSANDS STRANDED AFTER "NATIONAL" BOMB ALERT.

text.p: Thousands of freezing racegoers were left stranded and in consternation on Saturday, hours after a bomb alert caused Britain's Grand National steeplechase to be called off.
Police decided that 20,000 cars and coaches would have to stay overnight in compounds on Aintree racecourse in northwest England while further checks were carried out.
A police officer in a helicopter circling overhead told the crowds waiting below that the vehicles would not be released and urged them to make their way home.
Police in cars later told people who had long distances to travel that they could be bussed into the city centre for refreshments and promised that other arrangements would be made.
Racegoers expressed dismay after standing outside in blustery freezing conditions for around three hours while police and a bomb disposal unit carried out a series of checks.
Four hours after the warning phone calls were received, police and other emergency services were still on high alert.
But many people, stranded miles from their homes, pleaded with police and security officials to be allowed back to their vehicles. Others were worried about dogs left in their cars.
Up to 100 racehorses were believed to be still in the stables at the course.
There was also concern for elderly people suffering from the effects of the conditions and they were treated in an ambulance outside the main gate.
Frustration was increased for many people forbidden to use their mobile phones in case they triggered an explosion.

In one incident, 49 racegoers from the Plymouth area in southern England had to make emergency arrangements to try get to nearby Manchester. An hotel there was attempting to send a bus to collect them.
"They are getting very cold and very fractious", said organiser Christine Le Marchant.
